title: Five-plus units on low-density lots narrowed to corner lots
subtitle: Also: changes to the additional dwelling unit grant program, a removed Hanlon Creek business park item, and by-laws.
overview: Council voted to keep exploring whether five or more homes could be allowed on low-density residential lots, but narrowed the work to corner lots next to arterial or collector roads {{vote:m3}}. Staff will not draft Official Plan or zoning changes for now. They will refine the criteria and report back in the fourth quarter of 2026 {{vote:m5}}. The direction passed narrowly, with several councillors saying it is too soon after four units became permitted as of right.

Council also approved changes to the Affordable Housing grant program for additional dwelling units (ADUs) {{vote:m1}}. Homeowners can now get funding for up to three units on a property and for more than one project. Developer-led projects get higher construction funding, no cap on units, and tiered funding for water, wastewater and private utility upgrades. Staff said uptake has been low, and the program ends in December 2026.
Item 2.2, on Hanlon Creek Business Park Phase 3 housekeeping amendments, was removed from the agenda. Council also approved four by-laws and adjourned at 7:52 p.m.

decisions.detail: Council received and approved changes to the Affordable Housing CIP additional dwelling unit grant program, widening eligibility and raising funding in some cases {{vote:m1}}.

decisions.item: Limit five-plus review to corner lots
decisions.detail: Council amended the staff direction so that the suitability criteria for increased density would apply only to corner lots next to arterial or collector roads {{vote:m3}}.

decisions.item: Remove drafting of policy and zoning changes
decisions.detail: Council removed the clause directing staff to prepare draft Official Plan policies and zoning by-law amendments for five or more units {{vote:m4}}.
Council directed staff to continue evaluating five or more units on low-density lots, refine criteria for corner lots on arterial or collector roads, and report back in Q4 2026 {{vote:m5}}.

debate: A delegate on the ADU grant program supported the amendment but said that, for a detached backyard unit, the grant still leaves the owner with a net loss over the 15-year affordability term. They also raised the cost of upgrading the water service on a city street.

Councillors asked how the ADU grant program is monitored. Staff said owners submit an annual declaration of affordable rent and the city can request leases or receipts. Staff also said a sliding repayment schedule applies if an owner leaves the program early. One councillor suggested asking for supporting documents every year.

A delegate opposed to five-plus units said the term understates how much intensification could result, for example when a lot is severed and each new lot gets multiple units. The delegate also raised student housing, parking and compatibility, and asked why vacant serviced land or intensification corridors were not the focus.

Supporters of narrowing the review to corner lots on arterial or collector roads said it balanced adding housing against neighbourhood concerns. They noted the work is only further investigation. Opponents said the list of such roads is longer than many expect, and that owners can already seek a zoning amendment.

Some councillors wanted to pause until data from the four-unit permissions is available. They cited limited uptake so far and no way to monitor rents on new units. Staff said water capacity exists in the system today but is being tracked, and that individual streets may not have enough.
